title: Narada Departs
on_slide_text: After singing Rama's tale and receiving Valmiki's worship, Narada soared through the sky to his own realm. Left alone in his hermitage, Valmiki sank into deep thought, unaware that a tiny forest incident would soon awaken his great resolve to sing.
rationale: Opens on the hook — Narada's skyward departure leaves Valmiki alone, setting the quiet before resolve.

title: East-Facing Vision
on_slide_text: Facing east on a kusha-grass mat, Valmiki sipped water by rule and entered yoga, fixing his mind on Rama. By yogic power all stood living before him — Rama, Lakshmana, Sita and King Dasharatha with his wives, laughing, talking and moving.
rationale: Establishes yogic preparation and the living vision that grounds the whole composition.

title: Amla on the Palm
on_slide_text: Clear as an amla fruit on the palm, Valmiki beheld Rama's past, present and future, and all hardships borne in forest exile by vow-firm Rama with Sita and Lakshmana. With true vision secured, he resolved to compose the Raghu history, ocean-deep, ear-sweet, granting dharma, artha, kama and moksha.
rationale: Shows total trikala vision turning into resolve for ocean-deep history.

title: Prince of Virtues
on_slide_text: First he saw Rama's birth, strength, compassion for all, popularity, patience, truth and goodness. Then the journey with Vishwamitra, their dialogue and sacrifice-protection, the breaking of Shiva's bow at Janakpur, marriage celebration with Sita, and calm, radiant courage before Parashurama on the way.
rationale: Covers early-life virtues, Vishwamitra, bow, marriage and Parashurama as foundation.

title: Coronation Undone
on_slide_text: In Ayodhya preparations rose for Rama's coronation, but Kaikeyi's opposition halted all. The consecration broke, fourteen years of exile were decreed, and grieving King Dasharatha lamented and died. The people wept, yet Rama consoled them and sent them back, ending Ayodhya's happy life.
rationale: Marks the great turning point — blocked consecration, exile and Dasharatha's death.

title: Exile and Sandals
on_slide_text: On the forest path Rama met Nishadraj Guha and crossed the Ganga while Sumantra returned with the empty chariot to Ayodhya. After rest at Bharadwaja's hermitage, they built a leaf hut at Chitrakuta on his advice. Bharata came to plead return, Rama offered his father's oblations, and Bharata ruled from Nandigram in the sandals' name.
rationale: Traces the forest path via Guha, Ganga, Bharadwaja, Chitrakuta and Bharata's sandals rule.

title: Dandaka Trials
on_slide_text: From Chitrakuta Rama entered Dandaka where demon Viradha was slain, then met sages Sharabhanga and Sutikshna while Sita was adorned and blessed by Anasuya. Sage Agastya gifted a divine bow. Then Shurpanakha came, lost nose and ears, Khara, Dushana and Trishira attacked and fell to Rama, prompting Ravana's abduction plot with Maricha.
rationale: Apex beat: Agastya gifts the divine bow and Anasuya blesses Sita; other Dandaka encounters live in the caption text.

title: Golden Deer Loss
on_slide_text: Maricha lured Rama and Lakshmana far as a golden deer and died, while Ravana seized Sita. Rama lamented and searched. The wounded vulture-king Jatayu gave his life. Then came the demon Kabandha and the sight of Lake Pampa, where Shabari lovingly fed Rama berries and roots, and grieving Rama met Hanuman on Pampa's banks.
rationale: Apex beat: the fallen Jatayu gives his news to Rama and Lakshmana; deer-lure, abduction, Kabandha, Shabari and Hanuman live in the caption text.

title: Friendship and Fall
on_slide_text: Hanuman led Rama to Sugriva on Mount Rishyamukha, fear was removed and firm friendship formed. Then Sugriva dueled Vali fiercely and Rama slew Vali. Tara's lament pierced hearts and Sugriva was crowned. Rama halted for rains, burned lion-like with anger when Sita's search delayed, and Sugriva mustered the monkey army.
rationale: Captures Sugriva friendship, Vali slaying, Tara lament and rainy halt anger.

title: Leap Across Ocean
on_slide_text: Sugriva dispatched monkeys to all four directions, assigning each band its region, while Rama entrusted Hanuman with his ring as identity token. Searching with Jambavan, the monkeys found a cave, then fasted foodless on the ocean shore. There they met Sampati. Hanuman climbed a peak and leapt the ocean, spurning Mainaka's rest and defeating the shadow-catcher and Simhika.
rationale: Apex beat: Rama entrusts the ring and Hanuman leaps the ocean; search parties and sea-trials live in the caption text.

title: Night in Lanka
on_slide_text: By night Hanuman slipped into Lanka, learning how to bear himself when helpless, surveying tavern, women's quarters and inner palaces where Ravana and his Pushpaka appeared. In Ashoka Vatika he found Sita, gave Rama's ring and message. Demonesses roared, Trijata told her dream, and Sita entrusted her crest-jewel for trust.
rationale: Enters Lanka by night, Pushpaka sight, Sita found, ring exchanged and jewel received.

title: Fire and Hope
on_slide_text: Then Hanuman uprooted Ashoka Vatika's trees, guards fell and demonesses fled. The wind-god's son let himself be bound, then burned Lanka with terrible roar. Leaping back over the ocean, he rioted in Kishkindha's Madhuvana honey, consoled Rama and placed Sita's jewel in his hand, filling Rama's sinking heart with new hope.
rationale: Shows Vatika ruin, capture, Lanka burning and hopeful return with jewel.

title: Bridge to Dharma
on_slide_text: Rama sought the ocean's passage and under Nala's leadership a bridge was built. The monkey army crossed and besieged Lanka by night. Vibhishana sought refuge and showed victory's means. In fierce battle Kumbhakarna and Meghanada fell, at last Ravana was slain and Sita recovered in the enemy city. Vibhishana was crowned and Pushpaka appeared, dharma's victory touching all hearts.
rationale: Apex beat: under Nala's leadership the host crosses the bridge toward Lanka with Vibhishana received; battle and coronation clauses live in the caption text.

title: Crown and Renunciation
on_slide_text: After war Rama flew toward Ayodhya in Pushpaka, meeting Bharadwaja on the way, sending Hanuman ahead to Bharata. Then came the tearful reunion of Rama and Bharata and Rama's coronation. The monkey hosts were farewelled. Rama gladdened his subjects, yet for the people renounced Sita, leaving what remains of Rama's earthly tale to Uttara Kanda.
rationale: Apex beat: the tearful Rama-Bharata reunion before Ayodhya; coronation and subjects live in the caption text.

title: Hearing Versus Knowing
question: Why did Valmiki sit facing the east and seek to see in yoga what he had already fully heard from Narada?
answer: Hearing gives words which remain another's experience, while yoga turns them into direct seeing; Bharata's Nandigram rule sounds like policy when heard but appears as living brother-devotion when seen. East-facing seat, water-sipping and steady posture are not ritual but preparation of the creative mind where calm senses let truth descend. In an age crowded with information-Naradas we judge without pausing, so the practice is to sit ten minutes, behold the human side, and only then speak or write.
on_slide_text: He heard Rama from Narada, yet sat eastward to see for himself, for hearing is another's experience while yoga makes truth one's own direct seeing. When body steadies and senses calm, policy like Bharata's sandals-rule becomes living devotion, teaching us to pause ten minutes before judging news.
rationale: Pauses to distill why direct seeing must follow hearing.

title: God in Laughter
question: Why did supreme yogic vision show Valmiki not a supernatural light but humans laughing, talking and moving about?
answer: Truth was found not above but in the courtyard where Dasharatha laughs with his wives; divinity is not separated from humanity but lies in sustaining relationships. Seeing a great man laugh dissolves worshipful distance into understanding and kinship, which is the psychology of compassion. Hence do not idolize an ideal figure but observe one ordinary moment of fatigue, laughter or worry and learn by connection.
on_slide_text: Why no blinding light but a courtyard where Dasharatha laughs with his wives? Because godliness lives not in miracle but in sustaining relationships. Seeing a great man laugh dissolves worship into understanding, awakening kinship, urging us to learn from one ordinary human moment this week.
rationale: Draws the human-divine insight from the laughing courtyard vision.

title: Witness Not Fate
question: Does seeing past and future together like an amla on the palm prove that everything is predestined?
answer: The reverse is true: Valmiki foresees abduction yet Rama laments, performs Jatayu's rites and searches to Pampa, never a puppet. Total vision gives not fatalism but compassion, ending blame and beginning understanding through the witness perspective from above. Knowing time gives action meaning rather than flight, so when future-anxiety haunts, see the situation afar like an amla and ask what is right action now seen from the end.
on_slide_text: If Valmiki held past and future like an amla, is all predestined? No — Rama still laments, honors Jatayu and searches to Pampa, no puppet. Total vision breeds not fatalism but compassion and witness responsibility, asking us to view anxiety from the end and choose right action now.
rationale: Unpacks the amla simile as compassion, not fatalism.

title: Song Over Sermon
question: To grant dharma, artha, kama and moksha, why did Valmiki compose ocean-like poetry sweet to ear and mind instead of dry instruction?
answer: Humans change not by command but by rasa; Shabari feeding berries teaches no rule yet opens a scripture of devotion. Like the ocean with pearls, waves and depth, every reader finds according to thirst, and the modern mind melts by story not data. Scripture therefore becomes song that first seizes ear, then mind, then life, so to teach a value tell one true small lived story, not a lecture.
on_slide_text: After watching Rama's birth, exile, Jatayu giving his life and Shabari feeding berries, why sing instead of giving rules? Because a rule tells you to be good, but Shabari's berries let you feel love. So Valmiki wrote ear-sweet, ocean-deep song for dharma, artha, kama and moksha — to teach a value, tell one true small lived story.
rationale: Reflects why sweet ocean-like poetry carries dharma better than instruction.

title: Counting the Cost
question: Why did Valmiki retain the sting of Sita's renunciation after Lanka's victory and coronation instead of stopping at a happy ending?
answer: Valmiki's honesty holds subjects' happiness and Sita's renunciation in one breath, showing even the ideal king lives with a wound where dharma demands a price. Rama's care for the collective appears larger than private love, unsettling the idea that dharma only gives happiness. Behind every great success lies invisible sacrifice cropped from the poster, so a complete story counts cost with victory; honestly note one hidden sacrifice behind success and see if repair is possible.
on_slide_text: Why keep Sita's renunciation after victory instead of a happy end? Because Valmiki counts cost with triumph — even the ideal king bears a wound when dharma for the collective outweighs private love. Behind posters of success hides invisible sacrifice. This week write one hidden compromise behind your success and see if repair remains.
rationale: Closes on the sharpest insight — why Valmiki keeps the wound with victory.
